articles.title: ‘I’m looking for faces which surprise me’: how Richard Avedon photographed the soul of his subjects
articles.summary: Ron Howard’s illuminating Netflix documentary looks back on the career of one of America’s most inventive and versatile photographers. Richard Avedon had only taken a couple of frames when he accidentally hit his head on a light being held above him. The Dalai Lama burst into laughter.
body: Avedon’s assistant, Sebastian Kim, was baffled. “I was like, what the hell happened? There’s only four frames out of a roll of 12 frames,” he recalls in a phone interview. “I realised he knew at that moment that something had happened, a mistake had happened: he hit his head and the Dalai Lama lit up.”

Kim, 52, now an eminent photographer in his own right, is among the interviewees who feature in a new documentary, Avedon, directed by Oscar winner Ron Howard, which premiered at the Cannes film festival and is released on Netflix this week.

The film explores the six-decade career of the fashion and portrait photographer renowned for white backgrounds that stripped away distractions and for capturing figures ranging from Marilyn Monroe and Charlie Chaplin to civil rights activists, anti-war protesters and working-class Americans.

Avedon was raised in New York City. His father, Jacob Avedon, co-founded a specialty store on Fifth Avenue, which was lost overnight during the Great Depression. Avedon struggled academically, flunking out of high school despite winning a citywide poetry prize.

articles.title: Kiah Roache-Turner Reunites With ‘Furiosa’ Star Alyla Browne on ‘Horrifically Creepy’ Road Movie Horror ‘Don’t Look’: ‘There Are Scenes That Are Going to Traumatize People’ (EXCLUSIVE)
articles.summary: Australian genre filmmaker Kiah Roache-Turner (“Sting,” “Beast of War”) is set to direct upcoming horror “Don’t Look,” reuniting him with fast-rising star (and fellow antipodean) Alyla Browne (“Furiosa”).
body: “Don’t Look” is described as a “fresh take” on the road movie horror, where the “true source of fear remains elusive and unseen.” Speaking to Variety, Roache-Turner simply said it was “scary as all hell” with scenes are “going to traumatise people very deeply.”

Set against the backdrop of the Australian outback, the film follows 15-year-old Riley (Browne), travelling across the outback with her father when they come across two seemingly abandoned cars at an isolated desert crossing. When an invisible force drags her father away Riley finds herself in a life-or-death struggle against a terrifying creature that is only visible to its next victim.

Alongside Browne — who starred in Roache-Turner’s spider horror “Sting” and whose credits also include “Sonic the Hedgehog 3” and “Nine Perfect Strangers” — will appear alongside George Pullar (“Evil Dead Burn”), Masha Basman (“Bay of Fires”) and Stephen Peacocke (“Me Before You”).
Speaking to Variety, Roache-Turner discusses boarding the project and working once more with Browne.

articles.title: DC Studios’ New Boss Jeremy Latcham Has a ‘Guiding Light’ for Superhero Movies: Would My Grandma Like It? ‘You Have to Make Them for Everybody’
articles.summary: Jeremy Latcham is the new president and chief creative officer of DC Studios, taking over duties after James Gunn and Peter Safran’s four-year stint. So what does that mean for the future of the DC Universe?
body: “When we were making the first Marvel movies I would always be like, ‘I don’t know if my grandma would like that.’ That became a guiding light… it became the stand-in for ‘is this going to work for regular people outside the bubble of Hollywood?’ Latcham said over the summer while talking to Christian Broadcasting News (via GamesRadar ) about his previous comic book movie philosophy.

Latcham notably joined Marvel Studios in 2004 and rose to senior VP of production and development, working closely with president Kevin Feige to launch the Marvel Cinematic Universe as an associate producer on “Iron Man.” He went to co-produce “Iron Man 2” and executive produce “The Avengers,” “Guardians of the Galaxy,” “Avengers: Age of Ultron” and “Spider-Man: Homecoming.”

articles.title: ‘Without storyboards, I feel like I’m in Grand Central station in my underwear’: film fights back against AI
articles.summary: As Hollywood begins to adopt the technology, the professionals in most direct jeopardy are the illustrators mapping out directors’ first visions. They sketch out what could be lost.
body: Usually, storyboards are made together by a director, an artist and other crew members responsible for the film’s visual storytelling, such as cinematographers, editors, production designers, stunt co-ordinators and more. “I find it very fulfilling to make art in such a collaborative way,” says Alex Clark, a British storyboard artist whose recent films include Bong Joon Ho’s sci-fi comedy Mickey 17, adventure romance The Gorge and Louis Leterrier’s recent thriller The Last House. “It’s about people sitting down to discuss each other’s ideas. You might act things out, make sound effects, read dialogue. You develop a creative relationship with one another.”

articles.title: David Walliams' career and controversies including Britain's Got Talent and Little Britain
articles.summary: The entertainer shot to fame on Little Britain and also has best-selling series of children's books.
body: David Walliams has been accused of grooming young fans and harassing women in the workplace, after failing to stop the Guardian and ITN publishing claims against him.

A three-year investigation, external by the two news organisations alleged the Little Britain star and former Britain's Got Talent judge preyed on teenage girls as young as 15 and young women, external for sexual purposes.
He had sought a High Court injunction to prevent publication, with his lawyers arguing if allegations were made public Walliams would likely kill himself. The court refused the request.

Walliams has denied all of the allegations but in a letter to journalists working on the investigation acknowledged "at times I behaved thoughtlessly towards other people I had casual sexual relationships with".

articles.title: Traces of Justice review – ‘Chinese Sherlock Holmes’ at centre of arresting forensic cop thriller
articles.summary: Based on real scientist Cui Daozhi, this sharp feature has thumping set pieces and knotty puzzles set across 30 years of gripping cases. The latest from Chen Sicheng, prime mover behind the hit Detective Chinatown franchise, offers a disarming mix of propaganda, copaganda and gripping narrative.
body: Yet Chen’s impressively limber storytelling also accommodates thumping set pieces and knotty forensic puzzle-solving. Remaining necessarily alert to key details, Zhang, in a likable unshowy turn, really does look like someone who’s spent long afternoons studying fingernail structure. The character’s personal life soon drifts out of focus, but the wider picture compels: a culture both becoming more baroque in its sociopathy – the bus bombers are an Asian equivalent to Leopold and Loeb – and sharpening its eye. (End titles also cite the centrality of Cui’s work to China’s current surveillance schemes.) Chen is pursuing reassuring closure and creates an arresting, effective feature besides.

articles.title: Met Police investigating more 'potential criminal allegations' about Brand
articles.summary: Det Supt Andy Furphy says the force had received "several reports during the trial and since the trial".
body: The Metropolitan Police have said several people contacted them during the trial and following the conviction and sentencing of the disgraced comedian Russell Brand, "to provide information or report a potential criminal allegation".
A Met spokesperson said: "Detectives are assessing this information as part of their ongoing enquiries."

Speaking to BBC Breakfast, Det Supt Andy Furphy, who led the Brand investigation, said officers were "looking at exactly what we've got" and "whether they're information that points to behaviour or whether they could constitute a criminal offence".
Brand is already being investigated over rape allegations from two more women. He has been interviewed under caution in connection to those allegations.

articles.title: Katelin Arizmendi on Bringing a New Perspective to Action With ‘Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother’
articles.summary: Speaking to THR at TorunCamerimage, the DP discusses crafting the visual language of Bassam Tariq’s genre-bending thriller, starring Mahershala Ali as a devoted hitman balancing family life with vengeance.
body: In Bassam Tariq ’s Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother, cinematographer Katelin Arizmendi takes on the action genre for the first time, bringing a distinctive visual sensibility to a film that moves between crime thriller, family drama and spiritual meditation. At its center is Latif ( Mahershala Ali ), a devout Muslim and professional assassin whose world is upended by his wife’s death and the demands of caring for their three children, in particular the search for breast milk to feed his newborn daughter.

Speaking with THR at the TorunCamerimage festival, Arizmendi discussed finding that visual language with Tariq, the practical challenges of shooting the film’s elaborate action sequences and the experience of being a woman cinematographer working in a still very male-dominated field.
What was your first conversation with the director about the film? Was it about the visual design, or did you start with the story?
